title: ESO’s Very Large Telescope images the Medusa Nebula
caption: The Medusa Nebula, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
celestial: Medusa Nebula, Sh 2-274 · constellation Gemini · about 1500 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #80 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: This colorful cloud is the Medusa Nebula, also known as Abell 21 and Sharpless 2-274, in the most detailed image ever taken of it, captured by ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile.

The Medusa is the work of a star in its final stage. As the star at the nebula's heart entered retirement, it threw its outer layers off into space, and that material now forms the glowing cloud. Objects like this are called planetary nebulae. The name is historical and has nothing to do with planets. The hot exposed core left behind lights up the surrounding gas.

The Medusa also shows the Sun's distant future, because the Sun will eventually become an object of this kind, casting off its outer layers and leaving a small, hot remnant behind. The telescope recorded the nebula through broad color filters and narrow ones for oxygen and hydrogen light.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.91 x 7.20 arcminutes) and distance (1500 light years), the frame spans roughly 3 × 3.1 light-years. Its light set out about 1,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the FORS2 instrument on the Very Large Telescope, using B, V and R filters plus filters for oxygen and hydrogen light. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures on an 8-meter-class telescope collect far more light than the eye, so this faint nebula looks much richer than it would by eye.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.

alt: The Medusa Nebula, a colorful cloud of gas shed by a dying star.
